books.section: Topic 6.10 Development of the Middle Class
Social Criticism in the Gilded Age
Industrialization, Corporate Consolidation, and the Gospel of Wealth

primary_sources: Andrew Carnegie, “Wealth,” North American Review, June 1889

stimulus.text:
“The problem of our age is the proper administration of wealth, so that the ties of brotherhood may still bind together the rich and poor in harmonious relationship.... The contrast between the palace of the millionaire and the cottage of the laborer with us to-day measures the change which has come with civilization. This change, however, is not to be deplored, but welcomed as highly beneficial.”

“The best means of benefiting the community is to place within its reach the ladders upon which the aspiring can rise — free libraries, parks, and means of recreation, by which men are helped in body and mind.... Thus is the problem of rich and poor to be solved. The laws of accumulation will be left free, the laws of distribution free. Individualism will continue, but the millionaire will be but a trustee for the poor.... Of such as these the public verdict will then be: ‘The man who dies thus rich dies disgraced.’”

(Andrew Carnegie, “Wealth,” North American Review, June 1889)
stimulus.source_note: Andrew Carnegie, “Wealth,” North American Review, June 1889. Public domain; wording checked against the 1889 issue (archive.org scan) and the Norton Voices of Freedom reprint.

stem: Carnegie's idea appealed to many middle-class Americans because it

options.text: called for the government to seize all private fortunes at once
options.misconception: Carnegie defended private fortunes; he did not call for seizure.

options.text: seemed to reconcile great wealth with moral duty, without changing the system
argued that poverty was proof of moral superiority
options.misconception: Carnegie did not glorify poverty; he addressed the duties of the rich.

options.text: demanded that workers overthrow their employers at once
options.misconception: The essay urged giving, not revolution.

rationales.A: Carnegie leaves the laws of accumulation free. Seizure is the opposite of his argument.
rationales.B: The essay lets readers admire success and still demand duty: the rich keep their fortunes but must give back through libraries and parks. The system itself stays unchanged.
rationales.C: Poverty is not praised anywhere in the passage. The subject is the duty of the rich.
rationales.D: Nothing in the essay calls workers to overthrow anyone. It calls the rich to give.
rationales.general:
Ask what the idea lets its reader keep and what it asks them to add.
1. Carnegie keeps the system: accumulation and distribution stay free.
2. He adds a duty: the millionaire is a trustee for the poor.
3. Background from the books: the middle class valued respectability and moral reform, and liked a duty that cost the system nothing.
4. So the idea reconciles wealth with morality without changing the economy.
Remember: an idea appeals when it answers a worry without taking away what the reader values.
